newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EP committee head campaigns for legal prostitution.
newsitem.headline: EP committee head campaigns for legal prostitution.

text.p: It will not be possible to combat illegal trafficking in women unless voluntary prostitution is legalised, according to the new head of the European Parliament's women's rights committee.
"I think it's important to ensure the criminal part of prostitution is abolished and brought under control," Nel van Dijk told Reuters in an interview.
"But you cannot abolish prostitution altogether and anyway, why would you want to?" the Dutch Green Euro-MP said.

Women in legal brothels in Amsterdam earned good wages, paid taxes, got social security and could leave when they liked, while illegal prostitutes were trapped in the clutches of often violent pimps because they had no identity papers or wages, van Dijk said.
But she admitted Dutch and Belgian laws designed to offer some protection to women in the white slave trade had not stopped pornography and paedophile rings operating in either country.

The Euro-MP said she was glad European justice commissioner Anita Gradin had begun campaigning for EU-wide action to stop international trafficking in women and the associated violence but she felt the Swedish commissioner's approach was too narrow.
"The Commissioner does not accept calling prostitution work -- because it should be banned, because it is bad for women, because it is humilitating."

Adopting such a "moral and clean hands approach" had the effect of sweeping all prostitution under the carpet, ruling out any legal control over the business and giving more power to the illegal pimps, van Dijk said.

The Euro-MP said the women's committee also thought the Commission's definition of trafficking too narrow as it dealt solely with sexual exploitation and did not tackle the misery of children smuggled into Europe to work as domestic servants.
One of van Dijk's main priorities as committee chairwoman for the next two and a half years is to launch an EU-wide campaign to prevent violence against women.
Here too, Gradin's approach was "a bit Swedish", she said, as it attacked prostitution but glossed over wife beating.
The EU should also be tackling such horrors as genital mutilation and abuse of women by fundamentalist islamic regimes, the Dutch Euro-MP said.
This was not cultural imperialism, she argued.

"Women's rights are human rights and human rights are universal," she said, adding that increasingly stringent European immigration laws meant more and more women from third countries were being forced to return home to abusive regimes.
Closer to home, the women's committee will be pressing for changes in the EU treaty to outlaw discrimination on the basis of sex, van Dijk said.

"One of the key elements of equal treatment and equal rights is economic independence," she explained, because having independent social security benefits and equal wages made it easier, for example, for battered wives to escape.
The women's rights committee also wanted the member states to include in the revised EU treaty explicit provisions for positive discrimination.

Some member states had national laws permitting affirmative action but employers could challenge them in the European Court of Justice, and had done so successfully, because there were no provisions in the EU treaty, the Euro-MP said.
Women now make up a quarter of the European Parliament -- 166 of the 626 Euro-MPs. Van Dijk would like to see more women in top decision-making positions.
She also wants the women's committee to have a greater say on draft legislation dealt with by other parliamentary committees to ensure it reaches the statute books in an acceptable form.
Van Dijk said she was very keen to prevent other committees sabotaging a draft directive designed to place a greater burden of proof on employers in sex discrimination cases.
